group.passage: For more than five decades, a massive pit of fire has been burning in Turkmenistan’s Karakum Desert. Measuring around 200 feet across, the Darvaza gas crater, as it is officially known, is more popularly known as the “Door to Hell”, or “Gates of Hell.” The fire, boiling mud, and orange flames in the gigantic crater, form a unique spectacle, attracting curious visitors from around the world. Indeed, it is no ordinary crater. The fires are fueled by flammable methane gas from massive underground reservoirs, which is one of the largest in the world. The hot spots range over an area with a width of 60 meters and a depth of about 20 meters. While the true account of how the fires originated remains a mystery, one of the most popular theories is that the flames have been burning since 1971, when a Soviet drilling operation went awry, and the rig collapsed in the middle of the desert. The Soviets lit the collapsed area on fire to burn off the methane, assuming the blaze would only last a day or two. Local geologists, however, have argued the crater was formed in the late 1960s and didn’t ignite until the 1980s. Despite its origin, the crater is a simple geological anomaly: how the slowly escaping natural gas could have accumulated and burned without being extinguished by the wind remains still unknown. However, although the crater has fascinated the curious minds around the world, Turkmenistan’s President Gurbanguly Berdymukhamedov wants to put an end to it. He appeared on TV and urged officials to find solutions to extinguish the fire. “We are losing valuable natural resources for which we could get significant profits and use them for improving the well-being of our people,” said the president, citing economic and environmental reasons. The crater “negatively affects both the environment and the health of the people living nearby.” Previous efforts to quell the fire have failed. Although several proposals to put out the fire have been assessed, it is unclear which one will lead to success.
